title: IBM marked instructions apart from the data. The models are a preview.
friendlyTitle: IBM released a way to mark the task apart from the data. It is a preview.
summary: On 12 November, IBM released two experimental Granite 4.1 previews, at 3 billion and 8 billion parameters, trained to read and write LLMON. LLMON is a markup language whose structural markers are reserved tokens, not ordinary characters, so an instruction, a piece of data, and a requirement can be addressed separately. IBM says that on some indirect prompt-injection tests, attack success falls to nearly zero, while general ability stays close to the Granite 4.1 Instruct models. A toolkit is on GitHub.
friendlySummary: On 12 November, IBM released two small experimental models, at 3 billion and 8 billion parameters. They are trained to read a markup language called LLMON. It marks the instruction, the data, and the rules as separate blocks, using special tokens rather than ordinary punctuation. IBM says that, on some tests, hidden instructions inside data are mostly ignored. A toolkit is on GitHub.
whyItMatters: A smaller model often fails because a document, an old chat turn, and the real task look the same in the prompt. LLMON is an attempt to say which block to run, and which blocks to ignore. IBM says it is for exploration, not production. If your pipeline is JSON, the repo includes converters that turn JSON into LLMON and back without loss. A preview that ignores a hidden instruction in a lab test is not a guarantee about your documents.
friendlyWhyItMatters: Small models often mix up the real task with an old note or a document. This format tells the model which block to follow. IBM says it is for trying out, not for production. If you already use JSON, the toolkit can convert it without losing the structure. A lab result is not a promise about your own files.
